en: Itivuttaka 69: Tikanipāta, Second Chapter Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard: "Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is like a dry stick, the person who is like a lotus leaf, and the person who is like a lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a dry stick? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of hate, and he does not abandon that state of mind. He dwells with a mind full of ill will, and he does not abandon that state of mind. He dwells with a mind full of cruelty, and he does not abandon that state of mind. Just as a dry stick, when thrown into a fire, burns up quickly and is easily consumed, even so, monks, this person dwells with a mind full of hate... ill will... and cruelty, and does not abandon those states of mind. This, monks, is called a person like a dry stick. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus leaf? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of hate, but he abandons that state of mind. He dwells with a mind full of ill will, but he abandons that state of mind. He dwells with a mind full of cruelty, but he abandons that state of mind. Just as a lotus leaf, though water touches it, is not wetted by the water, even so, monks, this person dwells with a mind full of hate... ill will... and cruelty, but he abandons those states of mind. This, monks, is called a person like a lotus leaf. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of hate, but he abandons that state of mind; he dwells with a mind full of ill will, but he abandons that state of mind; he dwells with a mind full of cruelty, but he abandons that state of mind. Furthermore, he develops the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to mind and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. Just as a lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and stands unsoiled by the water, even so, monks, this person dwells with a mind full of hate... ill will... and cruelty, but he abandons those states of mind; furthermore, he develops the four bases of psychic power. This, monks, is called a person like a lotus flower. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, a certain monk addressed the monks: "Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and gone to his dwelling after saying: 'Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world... [as above]... These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Now, friends, what is the meaning of this statement? When this was said, another monk replied: "Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and gone to his dwelling after saying: 'Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world... [as above]... These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Now, friends, what is the meaning of this statement? When this was said, yet another monk replied: "Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and gone to his dwelling after saying: 'Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world... [as above]... These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Now, friends, what is the meaning of this statement? When this was said, still another monk replied: "Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and gone to his dwelling after saying: 'Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world... [as above]... These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Now, friends, what is the meaning of this statement?

The Second Discourse on Lust.
This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant; thus have I heard:
"Bhikkhus, for whatever bhikkhu or bhikkhunī lust has not been abandoned, hatred has not been abandoned, and delusion has not been abandoned—"
“Monks, this person is called one who has not crossed the ocean that is full of waves, whirlpools, crocodiles, and demons.

But for any monk or nun, monks, who has abandoned lust, abandoned hatred, and abandoned delusion—this person, monks, is called one who has crossed the ocean that is full of waves, whirlpools, crocodiles, and demons; who has crossed over and reached the further shore, the brahmin who stands on firm ground.”
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
“Whose lust and hatred, and...
And ignorance has been abandoned;
he has crossed over the pleasant ocean, with its crocodiles and demons,
its waves and fears, so difficult to cross.
Having transcended attachments, having abandoned death, and being free from acquisitions,
he has abandoned suffering for the sake of no further becoming;
having reached his final goal, he cannot be measured.
"I say that he has confounded the King of Death.
This matter was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
The tenth [sutta].
The Second Chapter.
Its summary:
Merit, the eye, and then the faculties.
"Truly, the two types of conduct are sorrowful:
that of the mind and that of passion.
Furthermore, they call the second group the supreme."
